profile.feeling: The speaker; the first word of every self-introduction.

senses.def: I (first person singular, masculine and feminine)
the ego, the self (as a noun: הָאֲנִי)

synonyms.nuance: the older Biblical “I”, used today only in elevated or archaic style (it opens the Ten Commandments: אָנֹכִי ה׳)

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔanāku, from Proto-Afroasiatic *ʔanāku.

funFacts: The Biblical form אָנֹכִי keeps the k of Proto-Semitic *ʔanāku, like Akkadian anāku; Arabic أَنَا (ʔanā) lost it, as did אֲנִי.
pitfalls: The present-tense verb after אֲנִי shows the speaker’s gender: a man says אֲנִי אוֹכֵל, a woman אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת.
subtleties: In the past and future the verb ending already means “I” (אָכַלְתִּי “I ate”), so אֲנִי is often dropped; in the present (a participle without person endings) it cannot be dropped.
As a noun, הָאֲנִי means “the ego, the self”.

profile.feeling: Direct address to one man or boy.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: Hebrew has no formal “you” (no T/V distinction like German du/Sie) — the same pronoun is used to a friend, a child, a boss or a minister; politeness comes from words like בְּבַקָּשָׁה, not from the pronoun.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔanta. Cognate with Arabic أَنْتَ (ʔanta).

funFacts: The dagesh in the ת is the trace of a lost n: Proto-Semitic *ʔanta became *ʔatta — compare Arabic أَنْتَ (ʔanta), which kept the n.
pitfalls: Masculine only: to a woman say אַתְּ. The verb agrees too: אַתָּה רוֹצֶה, but אַתְּ רוֹצָה.
Spelled with a final ה although it is pronounced atá.
subtleties: Hebrew has no polite “you”: אַתָּה is used to everyone, including strangers and superiors.

profile.feeling: Direct address to one woman or girl.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: Hebrew has no formal “you” (no T/V distinction like German du/Sie) — the same pronoun is used to a friend, a child, a boss or a minister; politeness comes from words like בְּבַקָּשָׁה, not from the pronoun.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔanti.

funFacts: Arabic keeps the vowel that Hebrew lost: أَنْتِ (ʔanti) ~ אַתְּ (at).
pitfalls: Without vowel marks אַתְּ is written את — exactly like the object marker אֶת. Only the context tells them apart.
The verb agrees: אַתְּ רוֹצָה (not אַתְּ רוֹצֶה).
subtleties: The final ת carries a dagesh and a shva — one of the few Hebrew words ending in a consonant cluster (at < *ant).

profile.feeling: A man — or any masculine thing (Hebrew has no “it”).

senses.def: is (present-tense copula linking subject and predicate)

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *šuʔa.

funFacts: Arabic هُوَ (huwa) is the same pronoun.
In the Torah scroll the letters הוא are also written for “she”; the vowels turn them into הִוא (read hi).
pitfalls: Hebrew has no neuter: a masculine thing is הוּא too — הַגֶּזֶר? הוּא פֹּה.
subtleties: In the present, הוּא can link subject and predicate like “is”: דָּוִד הוּא מוֹרֶה. It agrees with the subject: הִיא for a feminine subject, הֵם / הֵן for plurals.

profile.feeling: A woman — or any feminine thing.

senses.def: is (present-tense copula for a feminine subject)

examples.tr: She buys lettuce at the market.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *šiʔa.

funFacts: Arabic هِيَ (hiya) is the same pronoun.
In the Torah the word is usually written הוא and pointed הִוא — the scribes’ spelling for “she” in the Five Books.
pitfalls: Feminine nouns are “she”: הָעַגְבָנִיָּה? הִיא פֹּה (The tomato? It’s here.).
Do not confuse הִיא (hi, she) with הוּא (hu, he) — the letters differ only in י / ו.
subtleties: The verb after הִיא takes the feminine form: הִיא אוֹכֶלֶת, הִיא שׁוֹתָה, הִיא רוֹצָה.

profile.feeling: The group, the family, “us”.

senses.def: we (first person plural, masculine and feminine)

synonyms.nuance: the short form of formal writing and speeches (אָנוּ מוֹדִים … “we thank …”)
a rare Biblical variant

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *niḥnu. Cognate with Arabic نَحْنُ (naḥnu).

funFacts: Arabic نَحْنُ (naḥnu) is the same word without the initial a-; Hebrew נַחְנוּ also exists (rarely) in the Bible.
pitfalls: אֲנַחְנוּ has no gender; the verb shows it: אֲנַחְנוּ אוֹכְלִים (men or a mixed group), אֲנַחְנוּ אוֹכְלוֹת (women only).
subtleties: The stress is on the middle syllable: a-NACH-nu.

profile.feeling: Talking to a group — of men, or of men and women together.

senses.def: you (second person plural, masculine; also for a mixed group)

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym, and no polite plural either: אַתֶּם is the only plural “you” for men or a mixed group, to friends or to an audience.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔantum. Cognate with Arabic أَنْتُمْ (ʔantum).

funFacts: The dagesh in the ת is the trace of a lost n, as in אַתָּה: Proto-Semitic *ʔantum became אַתֶּם, while Arabic أَنْتُمْ (ʔantum) kept it.
pitfalls: A mixed group is masculine: talking to five women and one man you say אַתֶּם.
Casual speech often uses אַתֶּם for women too; standard Hebrew uses אַתֶּן for a group of women only.
subtleties: In the past and future the verb ending already says “you (pl.)” (הֱיִיתֶם “you were”), so אַתֶּם can be dropped there — but not in the present.

profile.feeling: Talking to a group of women only.

senses.def: you (second person plural, feminine: a group of women only)

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; there is no polite form either.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔantin. Wiktionary also gives the pointing אַתֵּן. Cognate with Arabic أَنْتُنَّ (ʔantunna).

funFacts: Arabic أَنْتُنَّ (ʔantunna) has the same feminine plural -n as Hebrew אַתֶּן and הֵן.
pitfalls: Only for an all-female group: one man in the group makes it אַתֶּם.
Unvocalized אתן is also אִתָּן “with them (f.)” or אֹתָן “them (f.)” — the context decides.
subtleties: In casual speech אַתֶּם often replaces אַתֶּן; in writing and careful speech אַתֶּן is expected.

profile.feeling: A group of men, or a mixed group.

senses.def: they (masculine plural, also for mixed groups)
those (distant demonstrative, after a definite noun: הַיָּמִים הָהֵם)

examples.tr: In those days there was no electricity.

synonyms.nuance: a longer Biblical variant

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šum. Cognate with Arabic هُم (hum).

funFacts: Arabic هُم (hum) is the same pronoun.
pitfalls: הֵם is used for any mixed group: nine women and one man are הֵם.
subtleties: With the article, הָהֵם means “those”: הַיָּמִים הָהֵם (those days), as opposed to הַיָּמִים הָאֵלֶּה (these days).

profile.feeling: A group of women only, or feminine things.

synonyms.nuance: a longer Biblical variant

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šin. Cognate with Arabic هُنَّ (hunna).

funFacts: Arabic هُنَّ (hunna) has the same feminine -n as Hebrew הֵן.
pitfalls: Only for an all-female group or feminine nouns; add one man and it becomes הֵם.
In casual speech many Israelis say הֵם even for women; written and careful Hebrew keeps הֵן.
subtleties: A homograph: the particle הֵן “behold; (formal) yes”.

lexemes.note: No present tense: in the present Hebrew uses a nominal sentence without a verb (הַמּוֹרֶה פֹּה “the teacher is here”). The participle הוֹוֶה exists only as a rare literary form, so only past, future and infinitive are stored. The past has person endings (הָיִיתִי “I was”); the third person agrees with the subject in gender and number.

override.V;PST;3;SG;FEM: Wiktionary lists the full and the vocalized spelling as one string “הייתה \ הָיְתָה”; we store the vocalized form הָיְתָה and the full spelling הייתה in plene.

profile.feeling: The invisible verb: everywhere in the past and future, absent in the present.

senses.def: to be (in the past and future; no present form in use)
with לְ: to have (in the past and future: הָיָה לִי “I had”)

examples.text: הוּא הָיָה מוֹרֶה וְהִיא הָיְתָה סְטוּדֶנְטִית.
examples.tr: He was a teacher and she was a student.

collocations.tr: to be or not to be

phrases.meaning: once upon a time — the opening of fairy tales

phrases.tr: what has been is what will be

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: הָיָה is the only verb “to be”; in the present Hebrew uses no verb, or a pronoun as copula (הוּא, הִיא, הֵם, הֵן).

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *haway- (“to fall, happen, be, become”).

funFacts: God’s name in Exodus 3:14 is explained with this verb: אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה “I will be what I will be”.
pitfalls: No present: “the salad is tasty” is הַסָּלָט טָעִים, with no verb at all.
Past and future agree with the subject: הַסָּלָט הָיָה, הָעַגְבָנִיָּה הָיְתָה, הַיְּרָקוֹת הָיוּ; הוּא יִהְיֶה, הִיא תִּהְיֶה.
In possession the verb agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner: הָיְתָה לִי עַגְבָנִיָּה (עַגְבָנִיָּה is feminine).
The past has a person ending, so the pronoun may be dropped: הָיִיתִי בַּבַּיִת “I was at home”; in the present the pronoun is needed: אֲנִי בַּבַּיִת.
subtleties: הָיָה + a present participle gives a habitual past: הוּא הָיָה אוֹכֵל … “he used to eat …”.
The everyday full spelling of הָיְתָה is הייתה.

lexemes.note: Written attached to the next word. Normative form וּ (u-) before ב, מ, פ and before a consonant with shva; before a hataf vowel it takes the matching short vowel (וַ before ־ֲ); before יְ it becomes וִי. The sentence bank uses וְ, and וּ before מ or a shva and וַ before a hataf patah (it avoids וּ before ב / כ / פ, which would also remove the dagesh of the next letter).

profile.feeling: The glue of every list.

examples.tr: Dad and Mum are at home.
I am a teacher and you (f.) are a student.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: וְ is the only “and”; גַּם means “also, too”.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *wa. Cognate with Arabic وَ (wa).

funFacts: Arabic وَ (wa) is written attached in the same way.
pitfalls: Before ב, מ, פ and before a shva the normative form is וּ: גֶּזֶר וּמְלָפְפוֹן; a following ב / כ / פ then loses its dagesh (לֶחֶם וּבָצָל).
Before a hataf vowel it copies the vowel: וַחֲצִילִים; before יְ it becomes וִי: וִירָקוֹת.
It is never written as a separate word.
subtleties: In everyday speech most people say ve- everywhere; u- is heard in careful speech, the news and reading aloud.
In pairs it is sometimes וָ: תֹּהוּ וָבֹהוּ, יוֹם וָלַיְלָה.

profile.feeling: An adult man — men and women, the sign on the door, and (in slang) a “real man”.

senses.def: dude, man (a friendly colloquial address: גֶּבֶר!)

examples.text: בַּכִּתָּה יֵשׁ עֶשֶׂר נָשִׁים וַחֲמִשָּׁה גְּבָרִים.
examples.tr: There are ten women and five men in the class.

synonyms.nuance: “a man, someone” (אִישׁ אֶחָד “a man, one man”); its plural אֲנָשִׁים means “people”, not “men”
a young man, a guy

etymology.text: From Proto-West Semitic *gabr-; compare Aramaic גַּבְרָא (gaḇrā, “man”). Root ג־ב־ר, as in the verb גָּבַר “to become stronger, to prevail”.

funFacts: The same root gives גִּבּוֹר “hero” and גְּבוּרָה “heroism”, and the name גַּבְרִיאֵל (Gabriel).
The feminine counterpart is גְּבֶרֶת “lady, Mrs.” — a speech opens with גְּבִירוֹתַי וְרַבּוֹתַי “ladies and gentlemen”.
pitfalls: “Men” is גְּבָרִים; אֲנָשִׁים means “people” (the plural of אִישׁ), not “men”.
The first vowel changes in the plural: גֶּבֶר → גְּבָרִים.
subtleties: On signs and forms the pair is גְּבָרִים / נָשִׁים (men / women); in polite address one says אֲדוֹנִי “sir” and גְּבִרְתִּי “madam”.
Calling a friend גֶּבֶר! is friendly slang (“dude!”).

profile.feeling: An adult woman; with “his / my”, a wife.

senses.def: wife (הָאִשָּׁה שֶׁלּוֹ “his wife”; with a suffix אִשְׁתִּי “my wife”)

phrases.tr: a woman of valour, who can find?
phrases.meaning: praise of a capable, devoted woman; sung at home on Friday evening

synonyms.nuance: “lady; Mrs.” — the polite word in address and titles (גְּבֶרֶת כֹּהֵן “Mrs. Cohen”)
a young woman, a “gal”

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʔanθ-at-. Cognate with Aramaic אִנְתְּתָא (ʾintəṯā) and Arabic أُنْثَى (ʔunṯā, “female”). Wiktionary notes that it is a false cognate of אִישׁ “man”: Semitic š and ṯ merged into Hebrew שׁ.

funFacts: Genesis 2:23 explains אִשָּׁה “woman” as taken from אִישׁ “man” — a famous wordplay; historically the two words come from different roots.
The true cousin is Arabic أُنْثَى (ʔunṯā) “female”.
pitfalls: The plural is irregular — נָשִׁים — and it stays feminine although it ends in -ִים: הַנָּשִׁים הָהֵן “those women”.
The modern full spelling is אישה (with י); the older spelling אשה is still seen.
subtleties: With a possessive it means “wife”: אִשְׁתִּי “my wife”, אִשְׁתּוֹ “his wife” (from the construct form אֵשֶׁת־).
The article takes a qamats before א: הָאִשָּׁה.

profile.feeling: Childhood, play, family — the everyday word for a kid.

senses.def: child, kid (the plural יְלָדִים is “children”, boys and girls together)

examples.tr: The children are playing in the park.
A boy and a girl are playing outside.

collocations.tr: a little boy, a small child

synonyms.nuance: a boy in his teens, a youth — older than a יֶלֶד
small children as a group (collective, formal)
“son” — the family relation, not the age

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *walad-. Compare Arabic وَلَد (walad, “child”), وَلَدَ (walada, “to give birth”), Ge’ez ወልድ (wäld, “child”). Root י־ל־ד “to give birth” (יָלַד).

funFacts: Hebrew turned a word-initial w into y: Arabic وَلَد walad ~ יֶלֶד yeled.
Turkish evlat “child, offspring” comes from Arabic أَوْلَاد (awlād), the plural of وَلَد — a cousin of יֶלֶד.
pitfalls: יְלָדִים means “children” (boys and girls together); for girls only say יְלָדוֹת.
The vowels change in the plural: יֶלֶד → יְלָדִים.
subtleties: יֶלֶד is both “boy” and “child”; when the sex matters, Hebrew contrasts יֶלֶד / יַלְדָּה.
Among adults it can mean “a kid”: הוּא עוֹד יֶלֶד “he’s still a kid”.

profile.feeling: A little girl — play, school, family.

senses.def: girl (of a young woman; affectionate or condescending)

examples.tr: We have a girl and a boy.
The girls are playing in the park.

synonyms.nuance: “daughter”; in the plural, הַבָּנוֹת is also everyday “the girls”
a girl in her teens, a young woman

etymology.text: The feminine of יֶלֶד (Wiktionary lists it as the feminine form), from the root י־ל־ד “to give birth”.

funFacts: Unvocalized ילדה is also the verb יָלְדָה “she gave birth” — the same root.
pitfalls: The plural is יְלָדוֹת (girls); יְלָדִים is “children” or “boys”.
The ד of יַלְדָּה has a dagesh (yal-da); the ד of יֶלֶד has none.
subtleties: Adults sometimes call a young woman יַלְדָּה — affectionate or belittling, depending on the tone (Wiktionary: “can be a compliment or an insult”).

lexemes.note: No plural in use: “people” is אֲנָשִׁים (or בְּנֵי אָדָם).

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses the noun אָדָם “man, human”; in Modern Hebrew it is the ordinary word for “a person, a human being” (אָדָם טוֹב “a good person”, כָּל אָדָם “every person”).

profile.feeling: A human being — neutral and a little serious; the warm everyday word is בֶּן אָדָם.

phrases.tr: it is not good for man to be alone
man is a wolf to man
phrases.meaning: people are cruel to each other (the Latin homo homini lupus)

synonyms.nuance: the everyday “person” (plural בְּנֵי אָדָם “people”); הוּא בֶּן אָדָם can also mean “he’s a decent person, a mensch”
“a man; someone” — and in counting crowds: מֵאָה אִישׁ “a hundred people”
“mortal, human” — poetic

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔadam-; compare Phoenician ʾdm (“man”) and Ugaritic ảdm (“man; red earth”). Wiktionary relates the word to *dam- “blood” and the colour red: Hebrew דָּם “blood”, אָדֹם “red”, אֲדָמָה “earth, soil”.

funFacts: Genesis links אָדָם with אֲדָמָה “earth”: the first human is formed from the soil.
Arabic آدَم (Ādam) is the same name; Turkish uses adam for “man, person” in everyday speech.
pitfalls: אָדָם has no plural in use: “people” is אֲנָשִׁים or בְּנֵי אָדָם.
With the article, הָאָדָם often means “man, humankind” in general, not “the person”.
subtleties: In speech the compound בֶּן אָדָם (often pronounced benadam) is more common than plain אָדָם for “a person”.

lexemes.note: Plural only: grammatically the plural of אִישׁ “man”, used as the plural of “person”.

override.meaning: Wiktionary files אֲנָשִׁים only as “plural indefinite form of אִישׁ”; its meaning in use is “people, persons”.

profile.feeling: Crowds, company, the people around you.

examples.tr: There are a lot of people here.

synonyms.nuance: “human beings, people” — stresses being human
“audience, crowd, the public”

etymology.text: Wiktionary files אֲנָשִׁים as the plural of אִישׁ “man” (and of the poetic אֱנוֹשׁ “human”, from Proto-Semitic *ʔināš-). אִישׁ goes back to *ʔinš-: the n lost in the singular shows up in the plural.

funFacts: Arabic إِنْسَان (insān, “human being”) and نَاس (nās, “people”) share this old root; Turkish insan “human being” is borrowed from the Arabic.
pitfalls: אֲנָשִׁים is the plural of אִישׁ “man” but means “people” (men and women); “men” is גְּבָרִים.
“A people, a nation” is עַם, not אֲנָשִׁים.
subtleties: When counting big groups, formal Hebrew uses the singular אִישׁ after the number: אֶלֶף אִישׁ “a thousand people”.

profile.feeling: Warmth and loyalty — friends, comrades, members.

senses.def: friend (male; the plural also for a mixed group)
member (of a party, club, the Knesset); comrade

examples.tr: I’m going over to my friends.
He is a member of the party.

collocations.tr: a member of the Knesset (abbreviated ח״כ)

synonyms.nuance: a friend in a more formal or literary register — also a safe way to say “just a friend”
“bro” — literally “my brother”, a friendly address
a companion, a fellow (Biblical and poetic)

etymology.text: Cognate with Arabic خ ب ر (ḵ b r) and Aramaic חבר. Root ח־ב־ר “to join, to be associated” (the verb חָבַר “to join, to be friends with”).

funFacts: Yiddish khaver “friend, comrade” comes from this word, and the slang חֶבְרֶ׳ה “the gang, the guys” goes back to Hebrew חֶבְרָה “company” through Yiddish khevre.
In the kibbutz movement חָבֵר also meant “comrade, member”.
pitfalls: With the article: הֶחָבֵר (not *הַחָבֵר), but in the plural הַחֲבֵרִים.
הֶחָבֵר שֶׁלִּי usually means “my boyfriend”; “a friend of mine” is חָבֵר שֶׁלִּי.
subtleties: The plural חֲבֵרִים covers a mixed group of friends; for female friends only, say חֲבֵרוֹת.

profile.feeling: A (female) friend — closeness, chats, company.

examples.tr: Sarah is a friend of mine.

synonyms.nuance: a (female) friend in a more formal or literary register — and a clear way to say “just a friend”

etymology.text: The feminine of חָבֵר (Wiktionary lists it as its feminine form), root ח־ב־ר “to join”.

funFacts: חֶבְרָה “company, society” comes from the same root: people joined together.
pitfalls: Unvocalized חברה is either חֲבֵרָה “a friend (f.)” or חֶבְרָה “a company, society” — context decides.
הַחֲבֵרָה שֶׁלִּי usually means “my girlfriend”.
subtleties: Women often call their friends הַחֲבֵרוֹת (“my girlfriends”) with no romantic meaning.

profile.feeling: School bags, classrooms, homework.

senses.def: disciple (of a teacher or a rabbi)

examples.tr: He is a pupil in the third grade.
The pupils go out for the break.

collocations.tr: a learned man, a Torah scholar

phrases.meaning: a learned man, a Torah scholar

synonyms.nuance: a university or college student — not a school pupil
a member of a youth movement, a trainee

etymology.text: From Akkadian talmīdu. Cognate with Aramaic תלמידא (talmīḏā). Root ל־מ־ד “to learn” (לָמַד), as in תַּלְמוּד “Talmud, learning”.

funFacts: Same root as the Talmud (תַּלְמוּד “learning”) and לָמַד “to learn”; Arabic تِلْمِيذ (tilmīdh, “pupil”) is a close relative.
pitfalls: תַּלְמִיד is a pupil at school; at a university you are a סְטוּדֶנְט.
A class of girls and boys is תַּלְמִידִים (masculine plural).
subtleties: In religious language תַּלְמִיד is a rabbi’s disciple; תַּלְמִיד חָכָם is a learned person, not “a clever pupil”.

profile.feeling: A schoolgirl — classes, notebooks, friends.

senses.def: pupil, schoolgirl (a female student at school)

examples.tr: She is a pupil in the third grade.
The (female) pupils are writing a test.

synonyms.nuance: a female university student

etymology.text: The feminine of תַּלְמִיד (from Akkadian talmīdu), root ל־מ־ד “to learn”.

funFacts: Israeli schools often write to mixed classes with both forms, e.g. תלמידים/ות.
pitfalls: A class of girls and boys is תַּלְמִידִים (masculine plural); תַּלְמִידוֹת is girls only.
subtleties: תַּלְמִידָה is a school pupil; a woman at a university is a סְטוּדֶנְטִית.

profile.feeling: Lectures, exams, cheap coffee — university life.

examples.tr: The students study in the library.
There is a discount for students.

synonyms.nuance: a school pupil (and a disciple) — university students are not called תַּלְמִידִים
“learner” — used in official texts

etymology.text: Internationalism, ultimately from Latin studens. Compare Polish student, Ukrainian студе́нт (studént).

funFacts: A word you already know: German Student, Russian студент; Greek says φοιτητής and Turkish öğrenci instead.
pitfalls: A pupil at school is a תַּלְמִיד, not a סְטוּדֶנְט.
The article doubles the ס: הַסְּטוּדֶנְט.
subtleties: The stress is on the last syllable: stu-DENT.

ref.note: Wiktionary has no page for סטודנטית; it lists סְטוּדֶנְטִית as the feminine of סְטוּדֶנְט.

profile.feeling: University life — from a woman’s side of the lecture hall.

senses.def: student (female, at a university or college)

examples.tr: The (female) students live in a flat.
I’m a student (f.) — do I get a discount?

synonyms.nuance: a schoolgirl, a pupil

etymology.text: The feminine of the internationalism סְטוּדֶנְט (Wiktionary lists it as its feminine form), made with the Hebrew suffix ־ִית.

funFacts: German Studentin and Russian студентка also make the feminine with a suffix — Hebrew ־ִית does the same job.
pitfalls: Plural סְטוּדֶנְטִיּוֹת: -ִית becomes -ִיּוֹת.
A mixed group of students is סְטוּדֶנְטִים.
subtleties: The feminine suffix ־ִית is the one Hebrew adds to many borrowed masculine nouns.

profile.feeling: Classrooms, chalk, patience — the man in front of the class.

senses.def: guide, instructor — in the construct form מוֹרֵה־: מוֹרֵה דֶּרֶךְ “tour guide”, מוֹרֵה נְהִיגָה “driving instructor”

examples.tr: The teachers at our school are good.

synonyms.nuance: the class (homeroom) teacher, responsible for the pupils — literally “educator”
“rabbi, master” — a teacher of Torah
a guide, an instructor, a youth leader

etymology.text: The present participle of הוֹרָה “to instruct, to teach” (Wiktionary), root י־ר־ה — the root of תּוֹרָה “teaching, the Torah”.

funFacts: “Teacher” and “Torah” are relatives: מוֹרֶה is “one who instructs”, תּוֹרָה is “instruction”.
Unvocalized מורה is also a verb form and an adjective (“rebellious”) — Wiktionary lists all of them.
pitfalls: The feminine מוֹרָה is spelled with the same letters (מורה): only the vowel, or the context, tells them apart.
Plural מוֹרִים: the final ה drops.
subtleties: Israeli pupils often call their teacher by the first name, or simply מוֹרֶה / מוֹרָה — Hebrew has no polite “you”.

override.gender: Wiktionary has no page of its own for the feminine מוֹרָה: it lists it on the page of the masculine מוֹרֶה (gender m), whose forms the check then compares.
override.N;PL;INDF: מוֹרִים is the plural of the masculine מוֹרֶה; the plural of מוֹרָה is מוֹרוֹת, which Wiktionary lists on the same page as the feminine plural.

profile.feeling: The woman in front of the class — and the word every pupil shouts.

examples.tr: She is a Hebrew teacher at the ulpan.
Most of the (female) teachers at the school are young.

synonyms.nuance: the class (homeroom) teacher
a kindergarten teacher

etymology.text: The feminine of מוֹרֶה, the participle of הוֹרָה “to teach” (root י־ר־ה, as in תּוֹרָה).

funFacts: Children in class simply call out “מוֹרָה!” — the word itself is the form of address.
pitfalls: מוֹרָה (mora) and מוֹרֶה (more) look the same without vowels: מורה.
Plural מוֹרוֹת; a mixed staff is מוֹרִים.
subtleties: As a form of address מוֹרָה needs no name or title: “מוֹרָה, יֵשׁ לִי שְׁאֵלָה” (“Teacher, I have a question”).

absent.reason: Hebrew has no neuter and no word for “it”: every noun is masculine or feminine, and a thing is “he” or “she”.
absent.use: הוּא for a masculine thing (הַסֵּפֶר? הוּא פֹּה “the book? it’s here”), הִיא for a feminine one (הַמְּנוֹרָה? הִיא שָׁם “the lamp? it’s there”); זֶה for “it” pointing at something or at a whole situation (זֶה טוֹב “it’s good”).

absent.reason: No separate word: the definite article ha- (הַ, also הָ / הֶ before gutturals) is a prefix and is stored in the DEF cells of every noun.
Hebrew has no indefinite article: a bare noun is indefinite (גֶּזֶר = a carrot / carrots). אֶחָד / אַחַת (“one”) can be added for emphasis.
